newsitem.title: USA: NYS eyes options after court rejects Medicaid rate.
newsitem.headline: NYS eyes options after court rejects Medicaid rate.

text.p: New York State said on Wednesday that it still was assessing whether to appeal or modify how it repays nursing homes for caring for Medicaid patients after a federal judge rejected the method it uses.

"We're looking at our otions now, both from a programatic side and legal side," said Bob Hinckley, a spokesman for the state Department of Health, adding the state had not set a deadline for reaching a decision on which tack it will take.

Judge Michael Telesca of the U.S. District Court in Rochester on February 12 held that the state had failed to support the method it used, and thus technically was in violation of the Boren amendment.

This federal law requires states to repay nursing homes for the "necessary cost incurred by an efficient and economically operated facility," Marc Carey, a spokesman Attorney General Dennis Vacco explained. He added that the state might elect to provide more data that would substantiate its reimbursement method.
The laywer who represented 96 nursing homes who had challenged the state's practice, Thomas Smith of Harter, Secrest and Emergy, in Rochester, was not immediately available to comment.
The judge directed New York State to find a remedy instead of ordering it to instantly stop the practice.

"Because this court has not reviewed the substantive adequacy of the rates at issue and New York does not have any rate system for which findings have been made in satisfaction of the procedural requirements of the Boren amendment, the use of the invalid reimbursement rates is not immediately prohibited," the judge wrote.

This apparant leeway led a state source to refute speculation that the court's decision would force Gov George Pataki to retreat from the big cuts in Medicaid that he fought for in his fiscal 1997 budget, as well as the even bigger reductions he proposed in his fiscal 1998 budget, which has yet to be approved.
"Not at this point, no," said the source, who declined tobe named. "He (the judge) has basically said that the state should redo its funding."
